questions.title: Basic SI unit
questions.question: Which one of the following is a basic SI unit?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Kilogram per cubic meter is a derived unit of density, built by combining two base units (mass and volume), not a basic SI unit on its own.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Kilogram per liter is a derived unit of mass concentration, likewise built from two base quantities, not a basic SI unit itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mole per liter is a derived unit of amount concentration, combining the base unit for amount of substance with volume, not a basic SI unit alone.
explanations.D: Correct. Meter is one of the seven SI base units, defining the fundamental quantity of length directly, unlike kilogram per cubic meter, kilogram per liter, or mole per liter, each of which is a derived unit built by combining two base quantities into a ratio. Base units are the small set from which every other SI unit is constructed by multiplication or division, which is exactly why meter alone, among these four choices, counts as "basic."

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify meter as a basic SI unit, distinct from derived/ratio units such as kilogram per liter or mole per liter.

questions.title: SI unit of temperature
questions.question: Which of the following is the SI unit of "temperature"?

explanations.A: Correct. Kelvin (K) is the SI base unit of temperature, defined on an absolute scale starting at absolute zero, and is the unit used throughout scientific and thermodynamic calculations even though clinical practice often reports Celsius day to day. Kelvin, not Centigrade/Celsius or Fahrenheit, is the internationally standardised SI unit for this quantity. It is the temperature analogue of meter for length or kilogram for mass — a true base unit, not a locally popular scale.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Centigrade (Celsius) is a widely used clinical temperature scale, but it is not the SI base unit — it is defined relative to the kelvin scale, offset by 273.15.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fahrenheit is a temperature scale used mainly in a small number of countries for everyday reporting, not an SI unit at all.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Joule is the SI unit of energy (including heat energy), not of temperature itself.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify kelvin as the SI unit of temperature, distinct from Celsius, Fahrenheit, and joule.

questions.title: SI unit of mass concentration
questions.question: Which of the following is the SI unit of "Mass concentration"?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Kilogram alone is the SI base unit of mass, but mass concentration is a ratio of mass to volume, not mass by itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Liter alone is a unit of volume, not a concentration, since concentration requires both an amount and a volume to be expressed together.
explanations.C: Correct. Mass concentration is defined as the mass of a dissolved solute per unit volume of solution, so its SI unit is kilogram per liter (or an equivalent scaled unit such as gram per liter, commonly used for clinical lab values like plasma protein concentration). It is built by dividing the base unit of mass by the base unit of volume, giving a single combined unit for this specific physical quantity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mole per liter is the unit of amount concentration (moles of solute per volume), a related but distinct quantity from mass concentration — amount concentration counts particles (moles), while mass concentration weighs them (kilograms).

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify kilogram per liter as the SI unit of mass concentration, distinguishing it from amount concentration's unit, mole per liter.

questions.title: Suffix for an immature, active cell
questions.question: Immature active cells are named with which of the following terminal (suffix) elements?

explanations.A: Incorrect. "-cyte" names a mature cell (for example, an erythrocyte or an osteocyte), the opposite maturity stage from what the question describes.
explanations.B: Correct. The suffix "-blast" names an immature, actively developing or actively dividing cell — an osteoblast is an immature bone-forming cell, and a fibroblast is an immature connective-tissue-forming cell. "-blast" cells are typically the precursor stage that later matures into the corresponding "-cyte" form once they finish differentiating. This maturity-stage contrast (immature "-blast" versus mature "-cyte") is one of the most commonly tested suffix pairs in introductory medical terminology.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "-genic" means "producing" or "originating from" (as in pathogenic, producing disease), describing a cause-and-effect relationship, not a cell's maturity stage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "-clast" names a cell that breaks down tissue (as in osteoclast, which breaks down bone), functionally the opposite role from a "-blast" cell that builds tissue up.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify "-blast" as the suffix naming an immature, actively dividing cell, distinct from "-cyte," "-genic," and "-clast."

questions.title: Meaning of "karyon"
questions.question: Which of the following best defines "karyon"?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cell membrane is named by a different root entirely ("cyt/o" combines with "-lemma" or "plasm/o" for membrane-related terms), not "karyon."
explanations.B: Correct. "Karyon" is the Greek-derived combining form for the cell nucleus, appearing in terms such as karyotype (the nucleus's chromosome set), karyolysis (nuclear breakdown), and the words eukaryotic/prokaryotic (describing whether a cell has a true nucleus). Recognising "karyon" as "nucleus" is foundational to reading any word that describes nuclear structure or nuclear disease processes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cell cytoplasm is described by the root "cyt/o" or "plasm/o," not "karyon," which specifically names the nucleus rather than the surrounding cell contents.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cell damage is not a defined meaning of "karyon" at all; "karyon" names a structure (the nucleus), not a pathological process.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Define "karyon" as the combining form for the cell nucleus, distinct from cell membrane, cytoplasm, or damage.

questions.title: Meaning of "Haemolysis"
questions.question: What is the meaning of Haemolysis?

options.A: Break down of red blood cells
options.D: Increase number of red blood cells

explanations.A: Correct. "Hemolysis" combines "hem/o" (blood) with the suffix "-lysis" (breakdown or destruction) to mean breakdown of red blood cells, with release of their intracellular contents (such as hemoglobin) into the surrounding plasma or fluid. This is a structural-destruction process, distinct from the body simply losing cells, forming new ones, or increasing the cell count. Hemolysis is the mechanism behind hemolytic anemia and several transfusion-reaction and inherited red-cell disorders.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Loss of red blood cells (as from bleeding) describes hemorrhage, not hemolysis — the cells leave the body or vessel intact rather than breaking down.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Formation of red blood cells is erythropoiesis, the opposite process from hemolysis (breakdown rather than formation).
explanations.D: Incorrect. An increase in red blood cell number is polycythemia, again the opposite direction of change from hemolysis, which reduces circulating intact red cells.

questions.subject: haem
questions.learning_objective: Define hemolysis as the breakdown of red blood cells, distinct from cell loss, formation, or increased count.

questions.title: Meaning of "hypoxia"
questions.question: Which of the following refers to hypoxia?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Increased carbon monoxide describes carbon monoxide poisoning, a different gas and a different mechanism from hypoxia, though severe carbon monoxide poisoning can secondarily cause tissue hypoxia by displacing oxygen from hemoglobin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Decreased carbon dioxide describes hypocapnia, a different gas from oxygen and not what "hypoxia" names.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Increased hydrogen relates to acidosis (a falling pH), an entirely different chemical measurement from oxygen level.
explanations.D: Correct. "Hypoxia" combines the prefix "hyp-/hypo-" (decreased, below normal) with the root "ox/o" (oxygen) and the suffix "-ia" (condition) to mean decreased oxygen — specifically, a reduced oxygen supply reaching the body's tissues. Hypoxia is a common final pathway in many respiratory and circulatory disorders, distinguishing it from other blood-gas or pH abnormalities such as hypercapnia or acidosis, which involve different molecules entirely.

questions.subject: cvs
questions.learning_objective: Define hypoxia as decreased oxygen, distinct from carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, or hydrogen changes.

questions.title: Meaning of "hemorrhage"
questions.question: Blood loss from a damaged blood vessel refers to which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hemolysis describes red blood cells breaking down, not blood escaping from a damaged vessel — a cell can hemolyze inside an intact vessel without any hemorrhage occurring.
explanations.B: Correct. "Hemorrhage" means blood loss escaping from a damaged blood vessel, whether internally into a body cavity or tissue, or externally through a wound. It names the event of blood leaving its normal vascular space, distinct from hemolysis (a cellular-level breakdown process) and from blood-pressure terms such as hypotension or hypertension, which describe pressure rather than the fact of blood escaping a vessel. Severe hemorrhage can secondarily cause hypotension, but the two terms describe different things — the bleeding event itself versus one possible downstream consequence.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hypotension means abnormally low blood pressure, a possible consequence of severe hemorrhage but not itself the term for blood escaping a vessel.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hypertension means abnormally high blood pressure, unrelated to the direct description of blood loss from a damaged vessel.

questions.subject: haem
questions.learning_objective: Define hemorrhage as blood loss from a damaged vessel, distinct from hemolysis, hypotension, and hypertension.

questions.title: Source gland of Epinephrine
questions.question: Which of the following describes Epinephrine?

options.A: A chemical substance produced by a gland above the kidneys
options.B: A chemical substance produced by a gland in the brain
options.C: A chemical substance produced by the skin
options.D: A chemical substance produced by a gland in the neck

explanations.A: Correct. Epinephrine (adrenaline) is produced by the adrenal medulla, the inner part of the adrenal gland, which sits directly above each kidney ("ad-" = near/toward, "ren/o" = kidney). The adrenal medulla secretes both epinephrine and norepinephrine as part of the sympathetic "fight-flight-fright" stress response, raising heart rate, blood pressure, and blood glucose to prepare the body for exertion. This gland-location fact — "above the kidneys" — is exactly what the word "adrenal" itself encodes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A gland in the brain describes the pituitary or pineal gland, not the source of epinephrine.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The skin does not produce epinephrine; it is not an endocrine organ for this hormone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A gland in the neck describes the thyroid or parathyroid glands, which secrete different hormones (thyroid hormone, parathyroid hormone) unrelated to epinephrine.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: Identify the adrenal medulla, a gland above the kidneys, as the source of epinephrine, distinct from brain, skin, or neck glands.

questions.title: Meaning of the prefix "chloro-"
questions.question: The prefix "chloro-" refers to which colour?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Yellow is named by a different combining form ("xanth/o"), not "chloro-."
explanations.B: Correct. The prefix "chloro-" means green, from the Greek "chloros." It appears in words such as chlorophyll (the green pigment in plants) and chlorosis (a historical term for an anemia that gave skin a greenish pallor). Colour prefixes like this are a small, fixed set that a terminology course expects to be memorised directly, since the prefix carries no other clue to its meaning beyond direct recall.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Red is named by "erythro-" (as in erythrocyte, red blood cell), a different colour prefix from "chloro-."
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pink has no standard single-word Greek/Latin colour-prefix equivalent taught alongside chloro-, xanth-, erythro-, and the other core colour prefixes, and is not what "chloro-" designates in any case.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Define the prefix chloro- as green, distinct from yellow, red, or pink.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-102 > Medical Terminology > Prefixes

questions.title: Meaning of the suffix "-stomy"
questions.question: The suffix "-stomy" means which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Cut in" describes the suffix "-tomy" (an incision), a closely related but distinct suffix from "-stomy."
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Removal" describes the suffix "-ectomy" (excision), again a related but different suffix from "-stomy."
explanations.C: Correct. The suffix "-stomy" names a surgically created permanent (or semi-permanent) opening, as in colostomy (an opening from the colon to the body surface) or tracheostomy (an opening into the trachea). It is easily confused with the similar-sounding "-tomy" (cutting into, without necessarily creating a lasting opening) and "-ectomy" (removing a structure entirely), so distinguishing all three suffixes by their distinct endings is a core terminology skill.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Visceral examination" is not a standard medical-terminology suffix meaning at all, and is not what "-stomy" designates.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Define "-stomy" as a surgically created opening, distinct from "-tomy" (cutting in) and "-ectomy" (removal).

questions.title: Meaning of the prefix "exo-"
questions.question: The prefix meaning outside or outer is which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Ana-" means up, again, or back (as in anaphylaxis or anabolism), not outside/outer.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Epi-" means upon or above (as in epidermis, upon the dermis), a different locative meaning from outside/outer.
explanations.C: Correct. "Exo-" means outside or outer, as in exocrine (secreting outward, through a duct, as opposed to endocrine, secreting inward into the blood) or exoskeleton (an outer skeletal covering). It is the direct opposite of "endo-" (inside/inner), and is distinguished from the other locative prefixes ana-, epi-, and dia- (through/across), which describe different spatial relationships entirely.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Dia-" means through or across (as in diaphragm or diarrhea), not outside/outer.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Define the prefix exo- as outside/outer, distinct from ana-, epi-, and dia-.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-102 > Medical Terminology > Prefixes

field_notes.keySource: digital highlight-box key on option C, render-confirmed (coverage/ZU-MED-102-triage.md)

questions.title: Meaning of the prefix "hemi-"
questions.question: "Half one side" means which prefix?

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Semi-" means partly or incompletely (as in semiconscious), not an exact half — a subtle but important distinction from "hemi-."
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Mono-" means one or single (as in mononucleosis), a numeric prefix rather than a fractional one.
explanations.C: Correct. "Hemi-" means half or one side, as in hemiplegia (paralysis of one side/half of the body) or hemisphere (half of a sphere, as in the cerebral hemispheres). "Hemi-" specifically denotes an exact half or one lateral side, which is what distinguishes it from "semi-" (partly, not precisely half) — a pairing frequently tested together because the two prefixes sound similar but carry meaningfully different degrees.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Di-" means two (as in diplopia, double vision), the numeric opposite of a fractional prefix like hemi-.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Define the prefix hemi- as half/one side, distinct from semi- (partly), mono- (one), and di- (two).

questions.title: Meaning of "Tachycardia"
questions.question: Tachycardia is a term describing which of the following?

explanations.A: Correct. "Tachycardia" combines the prefix "tachy-" (fast) with the suffix "-cardia" (heart condition) to mean abnormally fast heart rate. It is the rate-based opposite of "bradycardia" ("brady-," slow, plus "-cardia"), and is distinct from a term describing heart size, which would instead use the suffix "-megaly" (as in cardiomegaly, enlarged heart) rather than "-cardia" alone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Abnormally small heart rate" conflates rate with size and direction; "-cardia" combined with "tachy-" specifically names a fast rate, not a size change.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Abnormally large heart rate" again conflates rate with size; a large heart is cardiomegaly, a structural finding, not what "tachycardia" describes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Abnormally slow heart rate" is bradycardia, the direct rate-based opposite of tachycardia, not a synonym for it.

questions.subject: cvs
questions.learning_objective: Define tachycardia as abnormally fast heart rate, distinct from heart-rate slowness or heart-size changes.

questions.title: Meaning of the combining form "cephal/o"
questions.question: The combining form "cephal/o" refers to which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Abdomen is named by "abdomin/o" or "celi/o," not "cephal/o."
explanations.B: Correct. "Cephal/o" is the combining form for the head, as in cephalic (relating to the head), hydrocephalus (excess fluid within the head/skull), or the fetal "cephalic presentation" (head-first) in obstetrics. Recognising "cephal/o" as "head" lets a learner correctly parse any compound term built on it, regardless of which body system that term otherwise belongs to.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Neck is named by "cervic/o" (as in cervical, relating to the neck), a different combining form from "cephal/o."
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ribs are named by "cost/o" (as in costochondritis), unrelated to "cephal/o."

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Define the combining form cephal/o as head, distinct from abdomen, neck, and ribs.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-102 > Medical Terminology > Suffixes and combining forms

questions.title: Term for inflammation of the kidneys
questions.question: An inflammation of the kidneys is termed which of the following?

explanations.A: Correct. "Nephritis" combines the root "nephr/o" (kidney) with the suffix "-itis" (inflammation) to mean inflammation of the kidneys. The suffix "-itis" is a fixed, high-frequency word part meaning inflammation of whatever structure the preceding root names, so correctly identifying the kidney root ("nephr/o," as opposed to the appendix, liver, or bladder roots used in the distractors) is what actually distinguishes the four options, since all four share the identical "-itis" ending.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Appendicitis" is inflammation of the appendix (root "appendic/o"), not the kidneys.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Hepatitis" is inflammation of the liver (root "hepat/o"), not the kidneys.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Cystitis" is inflammation of the bladder (root "cyst/o"), not the kidneys.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify nephritis (kidney root + "-itis") as inflammation of the kidneys, distinguishing the root from appendicitis, hepatitis, and cystitis, which share the same suffix on a different organ root.

questions.title: Palm orientation in the anatomical position
questions.question: In the anatomical position, the palms of the hands are facing which of the following?

explanations.A: Correct. In the standard anatomical position, the body stands erect, facing forward, with the arms at the sides and the palms of the hands facing anteriorly (forward). This reference posture is what every other directional term (anterior/posterior, medial/lateral, proximal/distal) is defined relative to, so its own details — including palm orientation — are themselves foundational facts a terminology course tests directly.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Posteriorly (facing backward) is the opposite of the palms' true orientation in the anatomical position.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Medially (toward the midline) does not describe the palms' forward-facing orientation in this reference posture.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Laterally (away from the midline) likewise does not describe the palms' orientation, which is defined by the front-back axis (anterior), not the midline axis.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that the palms face anteriorly in the standard anatomical position, distinct from posterior, medial, or lateral orientation.

questions.title: Meaning of "distal"
questions.question: Which of the following describes movement or position away from the point of attachment or origin?

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Proximal" describes the opposite relationship — toward the point of attachment or origin — not away from it.
explanations.B: Correct. "Distal" describes a position or movement away from the point of attachment or origin of a structure; for example, the fingertips are distal to the wrist, and the wrist is distal to the elbow. "Distal" and "proximal" form a near/far axis specifically for structures with a point of origin (typically limbs), distinct from the front/back axis described by anterior and posterior, which is a different pair of directional terms entirely.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Anterior" describes a front-facing position, part of the front/back axis, not the near/far-from-origin axis the question describes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Posterior" describes a back-facing position, likewise part of the front/back axis rather than the near/far-from-origin relationship.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Define distal as movement/position away from the point of attachment or origin, distinct from proximal, anterior, and posterior.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-102 > Medical Terminology > Anatomical position and directional terminology

questions.title: Ureter destination
questions.question: The ureters, which are part of the urinary system, connect the kidneys to which of the following?

explanations.A: Correct. The ureters are the paired tubes that connect each kidney's renal pelvis to the urinary bladder, carrying urine downward by peristalsis for storage until voiding. This is the middle link in the full urinary drainage pathway — kidney, then ureter, then bladder, then urethra, then the exterior of the body — and is the specific link this question tests.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The urethra is the next tube in the pathway, carrying urine from the bladder to the exterior of the body — it is the ureter's downstream neighbour, not its destination.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The rectum is part of the digestive tract, entirely unrelated to the urinary drainage pathway the ureters belong to.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The intestine is likewise a digestive-tract structure, not part of the urinary system the ureters connect within.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: State that the ureters connect the kidneys to the bladder, distinct from the urethra, rectum, and intestine.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-102 > Medical Terminology > Urinary tract anatomy

field_notes.keySource: digital highlight-box key on option a, render-confirmed (coverage/ZU-MED-102-triage.md)

questions.title: Part of the gastrointestinal tube
questions.question: Which of the following is a part of the gastrointestinal tube?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The spleen is a lymphoid organ involved in blood filtration and immune function, not a segment of the gastrointestinal tube through which food passes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The gall bladder stores and releases bile via the biliary system, connecting to the digestive tract but not itself a segment of the tube food travels through.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The pancreas is an accessory digestive gland that secretes digestive enzymes and hormones into the duodenum via its own duct, but it too sits outside the food-passage tube itself.
explanations.D: Correct. The duodenum is the first, shortest segment of the small intestine, immediately distal to the stomach, and is a true part of the gastrointestinal tube through which food and chyme physically pass. Unlike the spleen, gall bladder, and pancreas — all commonly grouped with the digestive system but none of them a segment of the food-passage tube itself — the duodenum is the genuine continuation of the alimentary canal after the stomach.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: Identify the duodenum as a true segment of the gastrointestinal tube, distinguishing it from accessory digestive organs (spleen, gall bladder, pancreas).
